subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Congo Basin
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Congo Basin usable.

hook.text: The Congo rainforest is the second largest on Earth — and the least explored.

buildup.text: It spans six countries and stores more carbon per hectare than the Amazon.

discovery.text: Its peatlands alone hold 30 billion tons of carbon — equal to 20 years of US emissions.

twist.text: The Congo absorbs more CO₂ than it emits — one of the last forests still doing that.

climax.text: Logging roads are opening remote areas, threatening this critical carbon sink.

punchline.text: The world's most important carbon sink is also its most overlooked.

quiz.question: What makes the Congo Basin unique among major rainforests?
options: It still absorbs more CO₂ than it emits

details.summary: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest tropical rainforest, spanning six countries across Central Africa. It stores roughly 60 billion tons of carbon, supports endangered gorillas and forest elephants, and remains one of the few regions still absorbing more carbon than it emits.
details.whyItMatters: The Congo Basin is a critical carbon sink whose forests are increasingly threatened by logging, mining, and agricultural expansion. Losing it would significantly accelerate warming.
takeaways: Congo Basin forests cover roughly 2 million square kilometers
They absorb more CO2 yearly than the Amazon's remaining forest
Poverty drives deforestation more than large-scale industrial clearing

faq.question: Why does the Congo Basin forest receive less attention than the Amazon?
faq.answer: Political instability, remote access, and less satellite monitoring have kept the Congo under the radar. It also deforests more slowly than the Amazon, though the rate is accelerating as population and commodity pressures grow.

faq.question: What unique species depend on the Congo forest?
faq.answer: Mountain and lowland gorillas, bonobos, forest elephants, and okapi are among thousands of species found nowhere else. The Congo is one of the most biodiverse regions on Earth, with many species still undiscribed by science.
